name: Gastornis (Giant Bird)
fact: A giant flightless predator bird! Stood taller than an adult human, ran at 50 km/h, had a bite that could crush bone. For a while, these birds were the top predators on multiple continents.

name: Paraceratherium (Indricotherium)
fact: The BIGGEST land mammal ever — bigger than any dinosaur! A hornless rhinoceros relative with a 1-meter-long head. It disappeared about 24 million years ago. Evolution creates, then destroys.

name: Ambulocetus (Walking Whale)
fact: A whale that could WALK! Had hind legs and lungs, living part-time on land. In just 50 million years, a land mammal went back to the ocean and became completely aquatic. Whales are evolved hoofed animals!

name: Eusmilus (False Sabre-tooth)
fact: An early saber-tooth cat evolving from smaller cousins. Shows how evolution gave certain mammals giant canines to hunt. The arms race between predator and prey continues through the ages.

name: Hyaenodon
fact: One of the fiercest mammal carnivores ever — a nimravid like a saber-toothed hypercarnivore! Hunted cooperatively like modern wild dogs. Later replaced by true cats and dogs that evolved better hunting tactics.

name: Phenacodus
fact: Ancestor of ALL hoofed mammals! A small primitive ungulate leading to horses, deer, camels, whales, and cows. Shows that seemingly 'modern' animals have unrecognizable ancient roots.

name: Basilosaurus
fact: A terrifying early whale with a serpentine eel-like body that gives it its mistaken name - king lizard. Basilosaurus had tiny useless hind legs still attached to its hips. It ate sharks and smaller whales, making it the apex predator of Eocene seas.
know: This 18-m whale still had hind legs — about 35 cm long, with knees, ankles and toes, far too small to walk on. They are leftovers of an ancestry on land.

name: Andrewsarchus
fact: Known from only a single enormous skull, Andrewsarchus had the largest head of any known land mammal carnivore. It was a mesonychid ungulate, more closely related to hoofed animals and whales than to dogs. Whether it was an active hunter or a massive scavenger is still debated.

name: Uintatherium
habitat: Forests and floodplains of North America
fact: A rhino-sized browser with six bony knobs on its skull and two saber-like canine tusks on the males. Despite its fearsome horns Uintatherium was a pure plant-eater with one of the smallest brains relative to body size of any mammal.

name: Pakicetus
fact: The four-legged dog-sized ancestor of all whales. Pakicetus was a fully terrestrial mammal that waded into rivers to catch fish - like a furry hoofed otter. Its ear bones show the unique structure found only in cetaceans, proving it was a whale despite looking nothing like one.
know: It looks like a long-legged wolf — but its ear bone has a thickened shape found in only one other group of animals: whales. Its ankle bones link whales to the hoofed mammals; their closest living relatives are hippos.

name: Embolotherium
habitat: Steppes and open forests of Mongolia
fact: A brontothere - a giant rhinoceros-like mammal with a massive Y-shaped horn of solid bone on its nose. Males likely crashed into each other at speed during combat. It was one of the largest land mammals of the Eocene.

name: Titanoboa
fact: The largest snake ever found — as long as a bus and too thick to fit through a doorway. It hunted giant turtles and crocodile relatives in the first rainforest known.
know: Snakes cannot make their own heat, so their maximum size depends on climate. A snake this big implies the tropics averaged about 30–34 °C — several degrees hotter than today, only a few million years after the asteroid.

name: Eohippus (Dawn Horse)
fact: The first horses were the size of a fox, with four toes on each front foot and teeth for soft leaves, not grass.
know: The horse family is one of the best-documented evolutionary sequences there is: hundreds of fossil species over 55 million years show toes being lost, legs lengthening and teeth growing taller as forests gave way to grassland.

name: Aegyptopithecus
size: About 6–7 kg — the size of a house cat
fact: A tree-living, fruit-eating primate from just before monkeys and apes went their separate ways — close to the common ancestor of baboons, gorillas and us.
know: Skulls from Egypt's Fayum desert show forward-facing eyes in bony sockets and a brain larger, for its body, than earlier primates' — though still small. The Fayum was then a river delta in dense forest.

name: Purgatorius
fact: One of the oldest primate relatives, appearing within a few hundred thousand years of the asteroid. Its ankle bones show it climbed trees.

name: Plesiadapis
fact: A squirrel-like cousin of primates with rodent-like front teeth — found in both Europe and North America, then joined by land.

name: Darwinius (“Ida”)
fact: A complete young primate so well preserved that its fur outline and last meal of fruit and leaves survive.
debate: Announced in 2009 with great fanfare as a “missing link” in human evolution. Most experts place it on the lemur side of the family, not ours.

name: Onychonycteris
fact: One of the oldest bats. Its wings show it could fly — but its ears show it could not yet echolocate. Flight came first.

name: Icaronycteris
fact: An early bat with ears built for echolocation, already hunting moths in the dark.

name: Leptictidium
size: About 90 cm, most of it tail
fact: A small mammal that probably hopped on its long hind legs like a tiny kangaroo, with a twitching, trunk-like nose.

name: Diacodexis
fact: A rabbit-sized runner — one of the first even-toed hoofed mammals, the group that later produced pigs, cows, deer, hippos and whales.

name: Coryphodon
fact: A hippo-like grazer with a tiny brain. It lived even on Ellesmere Island in the Arctic, beside alligators — the Arctic was warm then.

name: Moeritherium
fact: An early elephant relative with no trunk and only small tusks. It probably lived half in the water, like a hippo.

name: Arsinoitherium
fact: Two massive hollow horns side by side on its nose. It looks like a rhino, but its closest relatives were elephants.

name: Dorudon
fact: A smaller whale that lived alongside Basilosaurus — and sometimes ended up as its prey: young Dorudon skulls carry Basilosaurus bite marks.

name: Archaeotherium
fact: A “hell pig” (entelodont) — not a true pig — with bony cheek flanges and a big appetite.
know: Bones of early camels found piled together suggest an Archaeotherium may have stashed carcasses to eat later.

name: Poebrotherium
fact: An early camel the size of a sheep. Camels evolved in North America and only later spread to Asia and Africa.

name: Mesohippus
fact: A three-toed horse the size of a collie dog, with longer legs and teeth for tougher leaves than the earliest horses.

name: Megacerops
fact: A huge rhino-like brontothere with a Y-shaped horn. The Lakota called the bones “thunder horses”.

name: Daeodon
fact: The largest entelodont, nicknamed the “terminator pig” — a bone-crushing scavenger as tall as a person.

name: Kumimanu
fact: The heaviest penguin known, described in 2023 — more than three times the weight of an emperor penguin, only a few million years after the dinosaurs died out.

name: Ectoconus
fact: Within a few hundred thousand years of the asteroid, mammals jumped from rat-sized to pig-sized. Ectoconus, a stocky plant-eater with clawed hooves, was one of the first big ones.
know: Its skeleton comes from rocks less than 3 million years after the impact. Comparing body sizes before and after shows how fast mammals filled the space dinosaurs left.

name: Taeniolabis
fact: A beaver-sized member of the multituberculates — rodent-like mammals with rows of bumpy teeth that lasted about 130 million years, longer than any other mammal group, before rodents out-competed them.
know: At Corral Bluffs, Colorado, fossil leaves and pollen show the forest recovering step by step after the impact — and mammals getting bigger as new plants appeared.

name: Champsosaurus
habitat: Rivers and lakes, even in the Arctic
fact: It looked just like a gharial — but it was not a crocodile. It belonged to an extinct group of water reptiles, and it lived through the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs.
know: Animals that lived in fresh water survived the impact far better than land animals. Rivers and lakes were sheltered from the worst cold and darkness, and their food chains started from dead plant matter, not living plants.

name: Carbonemys
fact: A car-tyre-sized turtle with a skull as big as a football and powerful jaws — big enough to eat crocodiles. It shared the swamps with Titanoboa.

name: Barylambda
fact: One of the first really big mammals — a heavy, ground-sloth-like plant-eater with a thick tail. It may have reared up on its tail and hind legs to pull down branches.

name: Titanoides
fact: A bear-sized plant-eater with long tusk-like canine teeth and big claws — weapons and tools on an animal that ate roots and leaves.

name: Mesonyx
fact: A wolf-like hunter with small hooves instead of claws — a meat-eater from the hoofed-mammal side of the family tree.
know: Its teeth look so like an early whale's that for decades mesonychids were drawn as whale ancestors. Ankle bones found in Pakistan in 2001, and later DNA from living animals, showed whales came from even-toed hoofed mammals instead.

name: Notharctus
fact: A lemur-like primate that lived in Wyoming when it was a tropical forest. North America had primates for 20 million years — and then lost them all.

name: Archicebus
fact: A primate small enough to sit in a teaspoon, and one of the oldest known. It mixes features of tarsiers and of monkeys, close to where those lines split.
know: The nearly complete skeleton was split between two slabs of rock. Scientists rebuilt it from hundreds of high-resolution X-ray scans at a particle accelerator in France (2013).

name: Indohyus
fact: A small, deer-like animal — and one of the closest relatives of whales. Its heavy, dense leg bones helped it wade, and its ear bone has the thickened shape found only in whales.
know: The living mouse deer of Africa dives underwater to escape eagles. Indohyus probably did the same — a hint at how the road to whales began.

name: Maiacetus
fact: A walking whale that still went ashore to give birth. One female fossil has her unborn baby inside — positioned head-first, as land mammals are born. Whales today are born tail-first, underwater.

name: Peregocetus
fact: A four-legged whale with small hooves on its fingers and toes, found on the coast of Peru in 2019. It proves early whales swam across the Atlantic from Africa to the Americas.

name: Janjucetus
fact: A baleen whale relative with no baleen — instead it had big eyes and sharp teeth for grabbing prey. It shows the giant filter-feeders came from small predators.
know: Found in 1995 by a surfer, Staumn Hunder, in a beach boulder near Torquay, Australia.

name: Pezosiren
fact: A sea cow with four working legs — pig-sized, able to walk on land and swim in the shallows. It shows how manatees and dugongs left the land.

name: Eurotamandua
fact: An anteater-like animal in Germany, with a long snout, powerful digging claws and no teeth.
debate: Is it an early anteater, a pangolin relative, or a member of an extinct group that evolved ant-eating on its own? It has been placed in all three.

name: Eurohippus
fact: A tiny early horse. One mare at Messel died while pregnant: X-rays show her foal in the womb — and the remains of the placenta, the oldest ever found.

name: Titanomyrma
fact: A giant ant — the queens were as big as a hummingbird.
know: The same giant ant turns up in Germany and Wyoming. To cross between them, cold-blooded insects needed warmth all the way across the Arctic — evidence of a short burst of extreme global heat.

name: Boverisuchus (“hoofed crocodile”)
fact: A long-legged crocodile that hunted on land, with toe claws shaped almost like hooves and blade-like teeth.

name: Inkayacu
fact: A giant penguin with a long, spear-like beak. Its fossil preserved feathers — and their colour: reddish-brown and grey, not the black and white of penguins today.
know: Microscopic pigment capsules in the feathers were compared with those of living birds (2010). Penguins' black colour, and the shape of their feather pigments, came later.

name: Phiomia
fact: An early elephant relative with a short trunk and four small tusks — two up, two down — feeding in the forests and swamps of North Africa.

name: Titanohyrax
fact: Hyraxes today are rabbit-sized. Their ancient relatives grew to the size of a rhinoceros, and for a while were Africa's main large plant-eaters.

name: Protoceras
fact: A deer-like animal with six bony knobs on its head — males had three pairs of horns, one pair right on the snout. Its relatives are closer to camels than to deer.

name: Pyrotherium
means: Fire beast — its first fossils lay in volcanic ash
fact: It had tusks and probably a trunk, and looks like an elephant — but it was a South American hoofed mammal with no close tie to elephants at all. South America, an island continent, grew its own versions of everything.

name: Torrejonia
fact: The oldest skeleton of a primate relative, 62 million years old. Its long fingers and mobile joints were made for climbing: the primate line lived in the trees from the very start.
know: Most early primate relatives are known only from teeth. This one has a partial skeleton, found in New Mexico, with the bones of its arms, legs, hands and feet.

name: Tsidiiyazhi
fact: A little bird from 62 million years ago, related to the mousebirds of Africa today. It could turn a toe backwards to grip branches. Bird families we know today began very soon after the asteroid.

name: Waimanu
fact: The oldest known penguin. It could not fly: its wings were already stiff flippers for swimming under water. Penguins gave up the air within a few million years of the asteroid.

name: Anthracosuchus
fact: A crocodile relative with a very short, blunt snout, from the same Colombian coal mine as Titanoboa. Its finders named it after the Balrog, the fire demon of The Lord of the Rings — because it came out of a deep mine.

name: Messel moths
fact: Tiny ridges on the scales of these moths’ wings are so well kept that scientists could work out their colour: a shining yellow-green, which probably warned birds that they tasted bad, and hid them among leaves while they fed.
know: The colour came from the shape of the scales, not from a dye, so it survived. Scientists measured the ridges with an electron microscope and calculated what colour light they would reflect.

name: Llanocetus
fact: An early relative of the baleen whales, about 8 m long — already a giant — with widely spaced teeth and no baleen. It probably sucked prey into its mouth. So whales grew big before they learned to filter-feed.

name: Saadanius
fact: A primate close to the common ancestor of apes and Old World monkeys, known from a skull found near Mecca. It lacks the bony ear tube that every living ape and Old World monkey has — a sign it lived just before those lines split.

name: Ucayalipithecus
fact: Teeth of a small primate whose closest relatives lived in Egypt — found in the Peruvian Amazon. It must have crossed the Atlantic, narrower then, probably on a raft of floating plants: the second group of primates known to have made the crossing.
debate: Rafting sounds unlikely, but there was no land bridge, and rodents made the same crossing. How long the trip took, and how any animal survived it, is unknown.

name: Rukwapithecus
fact: A piece of jaw with teeth, 25 million years old — the oldest known ape. The oldest known Old World monkey was found in the same rocks, so by then the two lines had already split.

name: Mammalodon
fact: A small relative of the baleen whales that still had teeth, and a short, blunt snout. It may have sucked its prey up from the sea floor. It lived in the same sea as Janjucetus — two very different experiments on the way to the great filter-feeders.
debate: Whether it fed by suction from the sea floor is argued from the shape of its skull; nobody has found its stomach contents.

name: Kairuku
fact: A tall, slim penguin with a long beak and long flippers — taller than an emperor penguin. Several kinds of giant penguin lived together off New Zealand.

name: Anthropornis
fact: A penguin as tall as a person, from an Antarctica that still had forests on its shores.

name: Sebecus
fact: A crocodile relative that lived on land, with a tall narrow head and saw-edged teeth like a meat-eating dinosaur’s. With the dinosaurs gone, its kind became South America’s top land predators.

name: Perupithecus
size: About the size of a squirrel
fact: The oldest known South American monkey — and its teeth match African monkeys of the time. Its ancestors must have crossed the young Atlantic on a floating raft of fallen trees.

name: Eritherium
fact: The earliest known relative of elephants: no trunk, no tusks, and about the size of a rabbit.

name: Cambaytherium
fact: A pig-sized animal close to the ancestry of horses, rhinos and tapirs. It suggests that whole group first evolved on India while India was still an island drifting north.

name: Vasuki
fact: A snake that may have rivalled Titanoboa as the longest ever, named after the serpent king of Hindu tradition.
debate: Only part of the backbone was found, so its length is an estimate with a wide range.

name: Eosimias
size: About 10 cm; would sit in your palm
fact: “Dawn monkey”: one of the earliest members of the group that includes monkeys, apes and us. It suggests our branch of the primates began in Asia.
